Heatmaps with ggplot2

R
ggplot2
Data Visualization
Heatmap
Tutorial
A step-by-step guide to building heatmaps from basic to advanced, perfect for visualizing patterns in matrix data
Author

Joao Luiz D’Andrea

Published

October 12, 2025

Introduction

Heatmaps are powerful visualizations for displaying matrix data where values are represented as colors. They excel at revealing patterns, correlations, and clusters in large datasets. In this tutorial, we’ll create increasingly sophisticated heatmaps using ggplot2.

We’ll explore correlations between vehicle characteristics and visualize temporal patterns in fuel efficiency using the mpg dataset.

What Makes Heatmaps Powerful:

Heatmaps excel at: - Visualizing correlation matrices - Showing patterns across two categorical dimensions - Revealing clusters and groupings in data - Displaying temporal patterns (time × category) - Comparing many variables simultaneously - Identifying hot spots and cold spots in data

Setup

First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)      # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(scales)         # For formatting
library(viridis)        # For color scales

# Prepare correlation data
# Select numeric variables for correlation
numeric_vars <- mpg %>%
  select(displ, cyl, cty, hwy, year) %>%
  na.omit()

# Calculate correlation matrix
cor_matrix <- cor(numeric_vars)

# Convert to long format for ggplot
cor_data <- cor_matrix %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column("var1") %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -var1,
    names_to = "var2",
    values_to = "correlation"
  )

# Preview the data
head(cor_data)
# A tibble: 6 × 3
  var1  var2  correlation
  <chr> <chr>       <dbl>
1 displ displ       1    
2 displ cyl         0.930
3 displ cty        -0.799
4 displ hwy        -0.766
5 displ year        0.148
6 cyl   displ       0.930

Chart 1: Basic Heatmap

Let’s start with a simple heatmap showing correlations between variables.

ggplot(cor_data, aes(x = var1, y = var2, fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile()                                       # Create heatmap tiles

Code Explanation

Line 1: ggplot(cor_data, aes(x = var1, y = var2, fill = correlation)) - Maps first variable to x-axis, second variable to y-axis, and correlation values to fill color

Line 2: geom_tile() - Creates rectangular tiles colored by the correlation values

What we have so far: A functional heatmap showing correlation patterns, but it uses a default color scale (blue gradient), lacks proper labeling, has no value annotations, and needs better formatting to be interpretable.

Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement

Now we’ll add better colors, value labels, improved styling, and meaningful axis labels.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

  • Diverging color scale (red-white-blue) for positive/negative correlations
  • Value labels showing exact correlation coefficients
  • White borders between tiles for clarity
  • Better variable names replacing technical labels
  • Correlation strength interpretation in colors
  • Title and context explaining the visualization
  • Legend improvements with better formatting
  • Axis text rotation for readability
# Create better variable labels
var_labels <- c(
  "displ" = "Engine Size",
  "cyl" = "Cylinders",
  "cty" = "City MPG",
  "hwy" = "Highway MPG",
  "year" = "Model Year"
)

# Update data with better labels
cor_data_labeled <- cor_data %>%
  mutate(
    var1_label = var_labels[var1],
    var2_label = var_labels[var2]
  )

ggplot(cor_data_labeled, aes(x = var1_label, y = var2_label, fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1.5) +    # White borders between tiles
  geom_text(
    aes(label = round(correlation, 2)),             # Add correlation values
    color = "black",
    size = 4,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#E76F51",                                # Red for negative
    mid = "white",                                  # White for zero
    high = "#2C5F8D",                               # Blue for positive
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-1, 1),
    name = "Correlation\nCoefficient",
    breaks = c(-1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1),
    labels = c("-1.0\n(Strong Negative)", "-0.5", "0.0\n(No Correlation)", 
               "0.5", "1.0\n(Strong Positive)")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Correlation Matrix: Vehicle Characteristics",
    subtitle = "Exploring relationships between engine specs and fuel efficiency",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Data: EPA fuel economy dataset | Values show Pearson correlation coefficients"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "#5A6C7D", hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 9, color = "#6C757D", hjust = 1, margin = margin(t = 10)),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank()
  ) +
  coord_fixed()                                     # Square tiles

Code Explanation

Lines 2-8: Creates a named vector mapping technical variable names to human-readable labels

Lines 10-15: Adds new columns with readable labels for both variables

Line 17: Maps data with readable labels to axes

Line 18: geom_tile() with white borders (1.5px width) separating each cell for clarity

Lines 19-24: geom_text() overlays correlation values (rounded to 2 decimals) as bold black text on each tile

Lines 25-34: scale_fill_gradient2() creates a diverging color scale: - Red for negative correlations - White for zero correlation - Blue for positive correlations - Custom labels explaining correlation strength

Lines 35-40: Comprehensive labeling explaining what the heatmap shows

Lines 41-52: Theme customization with angled x-axis labels, bold text, no gridlines, and centered titles

Line 53: coord_fixed() ensures tiles are square (equal width and height)

What we have now: A much more informative correlation heatmap with clear value labels, meaningful colors (red=negative, blue=positive), and readable variable names. The diverging color scale makes it immediately obvious which variables are positively or negatively correlated. The white borders and square tiles create a clean, professional appearance.

Chart 3: Advanced Visualization

Let’s create a publication-ready heatmap with clustering, dendrograms, and enhanced annotations.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

  • Hierarchical clustering to reorder variables
  • Significance indicators showing which correlations are statistically significant
  • Annotated insights highlighting key patterns
  • Lower triangular display avoiding redundancy
  • Enhanced color scheme with better discrimination
  • Correlation strength categories in annotations
  • Professional typography and spacing
  • Statistical context with p-values
# Perform hierarchical clustering to reorder variables
dist_matrix <- as.dist(1 - abs(cor_matrix))
hc <- hclust(dist_matrix)
var_order <- rownames(cor_matrix)[hc$order]

# Calculate p-values for correlations
library(Hmisc)
cor_test <- rcorr(as.matrix(numeric_vars))
p_values <- cor_test$P

# Convert p-values to long format
p_data <- p_values %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column("var1") %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -var1,
    names_to = "var2",
    values_to = "p_value"
  )

# Combine correlation and p-value data
cor_data_full <- cor_data %>%
  left_join(p_data, by = c("var1", "var2")) %>%
  mutate(
    # Reorder by clustering
    var1 = factor(var1, levels = var_order),
    var2 = factor(var2, levels = var_order),
    # Add readable labels
    var1_label = var_labels[as.character(var1)],
    var2_label = var_labels[as.character(var2)],
    # Determine significance
    significant = p_value < 0.05,
    sig_label = case_when(
      p_value < 0.001 ~ "***",
      p_value < 0.01 ~ "**",
      p_value < 0.05 ~ "*",
      TRUE ~ ""
    ),
    # Only show lower triangle (avoid redundancy)
    show_tile = as.numeric(var1) >= as.numeric(var2)
  )

# Filter to lower triangle only
cor_data_lower <- cor_data_full %>%
  filter(show_tile)

# Identify strong correlations for annotation
strong_cor <- cor_data_lower %>%
  filter(abs(correlation) > 0.8, var1 != var2) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(correlation)))

ggplot(cor_data_lower, aes(x = var1_label, y = var2_label, fill = correlation)) +
  
  # Add tiles with borders
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 2) +
  
  # Add correlation values with significance stars
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(round(correlation, 2), "\n", sig_label)),
    color = ifelse(abs(cor_data_lower$correlation) > 0.6, "white", "black"),
    size = 3.5,
    fontface = "bold",
    lineheight = 0.9
  ) +
  
  # Highlight diagonal
  geom_tile(
    data = cor_data_lower %>% filter(var1 == var2),
    color = "#2C3E50",
    linewidth = 3,
    fill = NA
  ) +
  
  # Add annotation for strongest correlation
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = which(var_order == strong_cor$var1[1]),
    xend = which(var_order == strong_cor$var1[1]) + 0.5,
    y = which(var_order == strong_cor$var2[1]),
    yend = which(var_order == strong_cor$var2[1]),
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm")),
    color = "#52A675",
    linewidth = 1.5
  ) +
  
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = which(var_order == strong_cor$var1[1]) + 0.6,
    y = which(var_order == strong_cor$var2[1]),
    label = paste0("Strongest: ", round(strong_cor$correlation[1], 3)),
    hjust = 0,
    size = 3.5,
    fontface = "bold",
    color = "#52A675"
  ) +
  
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#D32F2F",                                # Darker red
    mid = "#FFFFFF",
    high = "#1976D2",                               # Darker blue
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-1, 1),
    name = "Pearson\nCorrelation",
    breaks = seq(-1, 1, by = 0.5),
    labels = function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Correlation Matrix with Hierarchical Clustering and Significance Testing",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Variables reordered by similarity | Highway and City MPG are perfectly correlated (r = ",
      round(strong_cor$correlation[1], 3), ", p < 0.001)\n",
      "Engine size strongly correlates with cylinders | Significance: *** p < 0.001, ** p < 0.01, * p < 0.05"
    ),
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Data source: EPA fuel economy data | Lower triangle shown to avoid redundancy | Dark borders highlight diagonal\nVariables clustered using hierarchical clustering (1 - |correlation|) | White text indicates |r| > 0.6 | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    # Title styling
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 15,
      hjust = 0,
      margin = margin(b = 10),
      color = "#2C3E50",
      lineheight = 1.2
    ),
    
    # Subtitle with insights
    plot.subtitle = element_text(
      size = 11,
      color = "#5A6C7D",
      hjust = 0,
      margin = margin(b = 20),
      lineheight = 1.3
    ),
    
    # Caption
    plot.caption = element_text(
      size = 9,
      color = "#6C757D",
      hjust = 0,
      margin = margin(t = 20),
      lineheight = 1.2
    ),
    
    # Axis styling
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1,
      face = "bold",
      size = 11
    ),
    axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 10),
    
    # Remove grid and ticks
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    
    # Overall plot styling
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20)
  ) +
  
  coord_fixed()                                     # Square tiles

Code Explanation

Lines 2-4: Performs hierarchical clustering on variables using 1 - |correlation| as distance, grouping similar variables together

Lines 6-8: Uses Hmisc::rcorr() to calculate p-values for all correlations, testing statistical significance

Lines 10-19: Converts p-value matrix to long format for merging with correlation data

Lines 21-41: Combines correlation and p-value data, then: - Reorders variables by clustering - Adds readable labels - Creates significance indicators (, , ) - Filters to show only lower triangle (avoiding redundant upper triangle)

Lines 43-45: Filters to show only the lower triangular portion

Lines 47-50: Identifies the strongest correlations (|r| > 0.8) for annotation

Lines 54-56: Creates tiles with thick white borders

Lines 58-65: Adds text labels showing correlation values and significance stars; uses white text for strong correlations (|r| > 0.6) for better contrast

Lines 67-72: Highlights the diagonal with thick dark borders

Lines 74-92: Annotates the strongest correlation with an arrow and label

Lines 94-103: Enhanced diverging color scale with darker red and blue for better contrast

Lines 105-113: Data-driven title and subtitle with specific findings and significance legend

Lines 115-166: Comprehensive theme with professional typography, left-aligned text, and detailed caption

Final result: A publication-ready correlation heatmap with hierarchical clustering, statistical significance indicators, and only the lower triangle displayed (avoiding redundancy). The clustering reveals that related variables (like city and highway MPG) group together. Significance stars show which correlations are statistically reliable. The annotation highlights the strongest relationship. Perfect for research papers, technical reports, or data analysis presentations.

Comparison: All Three Charts

Here’s how our heatmaps evolved:

Aspect Basic Intermediate Advanced
Information Density Low (colors only) Medium (+ values) High (+ significance + clustering)
Color Scale Generic blue Diverging (red-white-blue) Enhanced diverging
Redundancy Full matrix Full matrix Lower triangle only
Statistical Info None Correlation values + P-values + significance
Organization Alphabetical Alphabetical Hierarchically clustered
Professional Use Not recommended Acceptable Publication-ready

Heatmap Variations

Different types of heatmaps for different data:

library(patchwork)

# 1. Calendar heatmap (temporal patterns)
# Simulate daily data
set.seed(42)
calendar_data <- tibble(
  date = seq(as.Date("2024-01-01"), as.Date("2024-12-31"), by = "day"),
  value = rnorm(366, mean = 100, sd = 20)
) %>%
  mutate(
    month = month(date, label = TRUE),
    week = week(date),
    wday = wday(date, label = TRUE, week_start = 1)
  )

v1 <- ggplot(calendar_data, aes(x = week, y = wday, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma", name = "Value") +
  facet_wrap(~ month, ncol = 4) +
  labs(title = "Calendar Heatmap", subtitle = "Daily patterns across the year") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

# 2. Categorical heatmap (class vs. manufacturer)
cat_data <- mpg %>%
  count(class, manufacturer) %>%
  mutate(class = str_to_title(class))

v2 <- ggplot(cat_data, aes(x = manufacturer, y = class, fill = n)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), color = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", name = "Count") +
  labs(title = "Categorical Heatmap", subtitle = "Model count by class and manufacturer") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

# 3. Binned heatmap (2D density)
v3 <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_bin2d(bins = 10) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "inferno", name = "Count") +
  labs(title = "Binned Heatmap (2D Histogram)", subtitle = "Density of observations") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11)
  )

# 4. Annotated heatmap with rankings
rank_data <- mpg %>%
  group_by(class, year) %>%
  summarise(avg_hwy = mean(hwy), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(class = str_to_title(class))

v4 <- ggplot(rank_data, aes(x = as.factor(year), y = class, fill = avg_hwy)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(avg_hwy, 1)), fontface = "bold", size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#E76F51",
    mid = "#F4A261",
    high = "#52A675",
    midpoint = 25,
    name = "Avg MPG"
  ) +
  labs(title = "Time Series Heatmap", subtitle = "Average highway MPG by class over time") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

(v1 | v2) / (v3 | v4) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Heatmap Variations for Different Data Types",
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust = 0.5))
  )

Variation Descriptions:

  • Calendar Heatmap: Shows daily patterns across months; good for time-based data
  • Categorical Heatmap: Counts or values across two categorical dimensions
  • Binned Heatmap: 2D histogram showing density of continuous data
  • Time Series Heatmap: Shows how values change over time across categories

When to Use Heatmaps

Heatmaps Work Well When:

✅ Visualizing correlation matrices - Perfect for showing relationships between many variables

✅ Comparing across two dimensions - Category × category or time × category

✅ Showing patterns in large datasets - Colors reveal trends quickly

✅ Displaying matrix data - Any data that fits in a grid format

✅ Identifying clusters - Similar values group together visually

✅ Time-based patterns - Calendar heatmaps for daily/weekly/monthly trends

Avoid Heatmaps When:

❌ Precise values matter - Hard to distinguish similar colors accurately

❌ Too many categories - More than 20×20 becomes cluttered

❌ Relationships aren’t gridded - Use scatter plots or networks instead

❌ Only a few data points - Use tables or bar charts

❌ Color perception issues - Ensure accessible color scales

❌ 3+ dimensions - Heatmaps are fundamentally 2D

Key Takeaways

Tips for Creating Better Heatmaps:

  1. Use diverging scales for correlations - Red-white-blue makes positive/negative immediately obvious

  2. Add value labels - Use geom_text() to show exact numbers on tiles

  3. Include white borders - Set color = "white" in geom_tile() to separate cells

  4. Make tiles square - Use coord_fixed() for equal width and height

  5. Consider clustering - Hierarchical clustering reveals natural groupings

  6. Show only lower triangle - For symmetric matrices, avoid redundancy

  7. Add significance indicators - Stars (, , ) show statistical reliability

  8. Choose colors wisely:

    • Diverging (red-white-blue) for data with meaningful zero/midpoint
    • Sequential (light-to-dark) for data ranging from low to high
    • Viridis for perceptually uniform, colorblind-friendly scales

  9. Label axes clearly - Replace technical names with readable labels

  10. Remove gridlines - Set panel.grid = element_blank() for clean appearance

  11. Adjust text color - Use white text on dark tiles, black on light tiles

  12. Consider ordering - Sort by values, clusters, or meaningfully

  13. Add context - Explain what colors represent in title/caption

  14. Test accessibility - Verify colors work for colorblind viewers

  15. Limit categories - More than 15-20 per dimension becomes unreadable

  16. Annotate patterns - Highlight interesting findings with arrows/text

  17. Use appropriate scales - Match color range to data range

  18. Include sample sizes - For aggregated data, show n counts

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Heatmap Pitfalls:

  1. Rainbow colors - Avoid “jet” colormap; use perceptually uniform scales

  2. No value labels - Readers can’t tell 0.7 from 0.8 by color alone

  3. Wrong color scale - Sequential vs. diverging matters

  4. Too many cells - 50×50 grid is unreadable

  5. No clustering - Random order hides patterns

  6. Missing zero - Diverging scales need midpoint at meaningful zero

  7. Inconsistent scales - Different heatmaps should use same color mapping

  8. No borders - Tiles blend together without separation

  9. Poor aspect ratio - Non-square tiles distort perception

  10. Ignoring redundancy - Full correlation matrix shows each value twice

  11. No statistical context - Show significance for correlations

  12. Inaccessible colors - Test with colorblind simulators

Advanced: Interactive Heatmap

For exploration, create an interactive version:

library(plotly)

# Create ggplot heatmap
p <- ggplot(cor_data_labeled, aes(
  x = var1_label, 
  y = var2_label, 
  fill = correlation,
  text = paste0(
    var1_label, " vs ", var2_label, "\n",
    "Correlation: ", round(correlation, 3)
  )
)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#E76F51",
    mid = "white",
    high = "#2C5F8D",
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-1, 1)
  ) +
  labs(title = "Interactive Correlation Heatmap") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
  coord_fixed()

# Convert to interactive
ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")
